title: Tetzaveh: Moses' name is missing
hook: Moses isn't named in this portion; some link it to his offer to be blotted out for his people (Exodus 32:32)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ner tamid, the lamp fed by crushed olives. Your line was crushed olives give light. Whose light did you honor? Today, still in Tetzaveh, something that isn't there. Day three hundred fifty-nine.

Look closely at the credits of a big movie and you'll find hundreds of names. But the person who stayed up all night fixing the sound in one scene might not be there. The neighbor who watched the director's kids for a year definitely isn't. Some of the most important work in the world is done by people whose names never appear. Since the night he was born in Egypt, Moses has been in almost every scene of the Torah. Pharaoh, the bush, the plagues, the sea, Sinai. And then comes this portion, Tetzaveh. Read it start to finish, and his name isn't in it once.
screen: `THE NAMES IN THE CREDITS.` → `THE ONES WHO AREN'T THERE.` → `TETZAVEH: NO MOSES.`

segments.voice: People who read the Torah closely have long pointed this out. From his birth in Exodus to the end of Numbers, Tetzaveh is said to be the one weekly portion where the name Moses never appears. He isn't absent, though. The portion opens, in Hebrew, v'atah tetzaveh: and you, you shall command. God is speaking to Moses the whole time. Make the oil. Dress Aaron. Ordain the priests. Moses is the you on every line. He's everywhere, and unnamed. Why? The Torah doesn't say. A medieval commentator, the Baal HaTurim, offers a striking answer. It looks ahead a few chapters, to the golden calf. After the people sin, Moses pleads for them, and says to God, in the old Jewish translation: "blot me, I pray Thee, out of Thy book which Thou hast written." Forgive them, or take my name out. The Baal HaTurim says the words of a righteous person carry weight even when said conditionally, and so his name was left out of one portion. Others notice that this portion is all about Aaron, his brother: Aaron's clothes, Aaron's sons, Aaron's role. Perhaps Moses steps back so his brother can stand in the light. Neither answer is in the text itself. But both point the same way. The greatest prophet in the Torah spends a whole portion as the unnamed you, doing the work, giving instructions that make someone else shine. His name can wait.
screen: `A PORTION WITHOUT HIS NAME.` · `V'ATAH: AND YOU, ON EVERY LINE.` · `BLOT ME OUT OF THY BOOK.` · `STEPPING BACK FOR AARON.` · then, large: `STEP OUT OF THE FRAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan a good deed without your name on it. Settle, and breathe. Think of something kind you could do this week where no one would know it was you. Paying for someone's coffee. Fixing something before anyone notices it's broken. Praising a colleague to their boss, out of their hearing. Sending money anonymously. Picture doing it, and then picture walking away without saying a word. Notice whether some part of you wants credit. That's normal. Let it be there, and do it anyway. The bell holds the time.
Tetzaveh. You shall command. The portion where Moses is the you on every line, and his name never appears.
Your line: step out of the frame. Today, do one good thing without your name on it, and let someone else stand in the light. Day three hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Jewish teachers often point out Moses' missing name when Tetzaveh is read; tradition also places Moses' death on the seventh of Adar, which often falls near this portion. Jewish law ranks giving anonymously among the highest forms of tzedakah.
